questions.q: Rewards are 1, 0, 2 and γ = 0.5. What is the discounted return from the first step?
questions.why: G = 1 + 0.5·0 + 0.25·2 = 1.5. Returns are easiest to compute backwards: G_t = r_t + γ G_{t+1}.

questions.q: What does the Bellman expectation equation for $V^\pi$ express?
options: The value equals the immediate reward only
A state's value equals the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state, under policy π
The value is the maximum over actions
The value is independent of the policy
questions.why: $V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a|s)\sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)[r + \gamma V^\pi(s')]$. The optimality equation replaces the average over π with a max.

questions.q: Why does value iteration converge for γ < 1?
options: The Bellman optimality operator is a γ-contraction in the max norm
It solves a linear system exactly
questions.why: The distance to the fixed point shrinks by at least a factor γ per sweep, so errors decay geometrically.

questions.q: How does policy iteration differ from value iteration?
options: It alternates full policy evaluation with greedy improvement, usually converging in few iterations
It works only for deterministic MDPs
It doesn't need a model of the environment
questions.why: Each improvement step gives a policy at least as good. Because there are finitely many deterministic policies, it terminates.

questions.q: In a continuing task with γ = 0.99 and reward 1 every step, what is the value of any state?
questions.why: The geometric series gives 1/(1 - γ) = 100. That is why 1/(1 - γ) is called the effective horizon.

questions.q: What is the relationship between $V^*$ and $Q^*$?
questions.why: The optimal value of a state is the value of its best action. Greedy action selection with respect to $Q^*$ is optimal.

questions.q: Dynamic programming methods like value iteration need what that model-free methods don't?
options: The transition probabilities and reward function
questions.why: DP sweeps over all successor states using the known model. Model-free methods estimate the same quantities from sampled experience.

questions.q: What is a stopping criterion commonly used for value iteration?
options: Stop when the policy is random
Stop when the largest change in any state's value in a sweep falls below a threshold
Stop when all values are positive
questions.why: A small max-norm change bounds the distance to the optimum by roughly $\epsilon\gamma/(1-\gamma)$.

questions.q: First-visit Monte Carlo evaluation updates V(s) using what?
options: The return following the first time s is visited in each episode
questions.why: MC waits for the episode to end and uses full returns. It is unbiased but can have high variance.

questions.q: The TD(0) update is $V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha[r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)]$. What is the bracket called?
options: The advantage of the best action
questions.why: TD bootstraps from its own estimate of the next state, trading some bias for much lower variance than MC.

questions.q: What makes SARSA on-policy?
options: Its target uses the max over next actions
Its target uses Q(s', a') for the action a' the current policy actually takes next
questions.why: SARSA learns the value of the behaviour policy, including its exploration. Q-learning's max learns the greedy policy regardless of behaviour.

questions.q: On the cliff-walking task with ε-greedy exploration, why does SARSA learn a safer path than Q-learning?
options: SARSA accounts for the chance of a random step off the cliff; Q-learning values the optimal path as if it acts greedily
SARSA has a larger learning rate
questions.why: Q-learning learns the shortest path along the edge, which is optimal for a greedy agent but falls off often while exploring.

questions.q: What target does Q-learning use?
options: $r + \gamma Q(s', a')$ for the taken action
questions.why: Taking the max makes it off-policy: it learns about the greedy policy while following any sufficiently exploratory one.

questions.q: What does Expected SARSA replace the sampled next action with?
options: The expectation of Q(s', ·) under the current policy
questions.why: Averaging over next actions removes the variance from sampling a'. With a greedy target policy it reduces to Q-learning.

questions.q: Why does the max in Q-learning cause overestimation?
options: The learning rate is too small
The max of noisy estimates is biased upward, since $E[\max_a \hat Q] \ge \max_a E[\hat Q]$
questions.why: Double Q-learning uses one estimate to pick the action and another to evaluate it, which removes most of this bias.

questions.q: Compared with Monte Carlo, what is TD's main advantage?
options: It works only for continuing tasks
It can learn online from incomplete episodes, with lower variance
questions.why: TD updates after every step. Its bias comes from bootstrapping off current estimates, which shrinks as they improve.

questions.q: Why is a purely greedy bandit strategy risky?
options: An early unlucky estimate can stop it ever trying the arm that is actually best
It always picks the last arm
questions.why: Greedy never revisits arms it currently underrates. Some exploration, even ε-greedy, keeps estimates honest.

questions.q: UCB1 picks the arm maximising $\hat\mu_a + \sqrt{2\ln t / n_a}$. What does the second term do?
options: Gives a bonus to arms tried less often, shrinking as they are pulled
questions.why: This is optimism in the face of uncertainty. UCB1's regret grows logarithmically in t.

questions.q: In Thompson sampling for Bernoulli arms with Beta priors, how is an arm chosen?
options: Draw one sample from each arm's Beta posterior and pull the arm with the largest sample
Pick the arm with the highest posterior mean
Pick the arm with the most pulls
questions.why: Arms with uncertain posteriors sometimes produce high samples and get explored. After a success the arm's α grows by 1; after a failure β grows by 1.

questions.q: What is regret in a bandit problem?
options: The reward of the worst arm
The total reward lost compared with always pulling the best arm
questions.why: Regret after T steps is $T\mu^* - \sum_t \mu_{a_t}$. Good algorithms keep it sublinear in T.

questions.q: In softmax (Boltzmann) exploration, what happens as the temperature goes to zero?
questions.why: Probabilities are proportional to exp(Q/τ). Small τ sharpens them onto the best arm; large τ flattens them.

questions.q: What does LinUCB assume about the reward?
options: The reward depends only on the time step
The expected reward is linear in a context feature vector, with per-arm (or shared) weights
questions.why: It keeps a ridge-regression estimate and adds a confidence bonus $\alpha\sqrt{x^\top A^{-1} x}$ from the design matrix.

questions.q: Why does fixed ε-greedy have linear regret?
options: It always picks the worst arm
It keeps exploring at rate ε forever, losing a constant amount per step on random pulls
questions.why: Decaying ε over time (for example proportional to 1/t) can fix this.

questions.q: What is the exploration-exploitation trade-off?
options: Choosing between a large and a small model
Choosing between on-policy and off-policy learning
Choosing between actions known to be good and actions whose value is still uncertain
questions.why: Too little exploration risks missing better options; too much wastes reward on options already known to be poor.

questions.q: Why does DQN use a separate target network?
options: To keep the regression target fixed for a while, so the network isn't chasing a target that moves with every update
questions.why: The target network is copied from the online network every few thousand steps, or updated slowly with Polyak averaging.

questions.q: What problem does experience replay address?
options: Consecutive transitions are strongly correlated; sampling from a buffer breaks that correlation and reuses data
It removes the need for exploration
questions.why: Random minibatches look closer to the i.i.d. data that SGD expects. Replay makes DQN off-policy, which is fine for Q-learning.

questions.q: In prioritised experience replay, why are importance-sampling weights used?
options: Sampling by priority changes the data distribution, so weights correct the bias in the update
questions.why: Weights $(N \cdot P(i))^{-\beta}$ are normalised by their max, and β is annealed to 1 so the correction is complete by the end of training.

questions.q: What is the Double DQN target?
options: $r + \gamma Q_{online}(s', a)$ for a random a
questions.why: The online network picks the action and the target network evaluates it, which reduces overestimation.

questions.q: The dueling architecture writes Q as V(s) + A(s, a) - mean_a A(s, a). Why subtract the mean?
options: Without it V and A are not identifiable, since a constant can move between them
To speed up the forward pass
To make A equal to Q
questions.why: Subtracting the mean (or max) of A pins down the split, which stabilises learning.

questions.q: For a terminal transition, what should the DQN target be?
options: Just the reward r, with no bootstrap term
r + γ max Q(s', ·) as usual
The maximum Q-value in the batch
questions.why: There is no future after a terminal state. Forgetting the done mask is a common bug that leaks value across episode boundaries.

questions.q: Why is the Huber loss often used in DQN instead of squared error?
options: It is linear for large errors, so rare large TD errors don't produce huge gradients
It makes the loss convex for neural networks
questions.why: Huber behaves like squared error near zero and like absolute error far away, similar to clipping the gradient of the TD error.

questions.q: DQN works for discrete actions. Why doesn't it extend directly to continuous actions?
options: The replay buffer can't store them
Neural networks can't output continuous values
The target and greedy policy need a max over actions, which is an optimisation problem in a continuous space
questions.why: Methods such as DDPG or SAC learn an actor that outputs the action, so the max isn't needed.

questions.q: The REINFORCE gradient estimate is $\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t) \, G_t$. Why does this work without differentiating the environment?
options: The log-derivative trick moves the gradient onto the policy's log-probability, which we can differentiate
It uses a model of the dynamics
questions.why: $\nabla E_\pi[G] = E_\pi[G \nabla \log \pi]$. Only the policy's own probabilities need gradients.

questions.q: Why does subtracting a baseline b(s) from the return not bias the policy gradient?
options: $E_{a\sim\pi}[\nabla \log \pi(a|s)]\,b(s) = 0$, since the score function has zero mean
questions.why: The baseline doesn't change the expected gradient but can greatly reduce its variance. A learned V(s) is the usual choice.

questions.q: In GAE, what does λ trade off?
options: Bias and variance: λ = 0 gives the one-step TD advantage, λ = 1 gives the Monte Carlo advantage
The learning rates of actor and critic
questions.why: $A_t = \sum_k (\gamma\lambda)^k \delta_{t+k}$, a geometric mix of n-step advantages.

questions.q: Why is an entropy bonus added to actor-critic losses?
options: To speed up the forward pass
To make the critic more accurate
To keep the policy from becoming deterministic too early, so it keeps exploring
questions.why: Maximising entropy pushes probabilities apart from zero. Its coefficient is usually small and sometimes decayed.

questions.q: In the A2C loss, how is the critic trained?
options: By regressing V(s) toward a return or bootstrapped target with squared error
questions.why: The critic supplies the baseline or advantage. Its gradient should not flow into the advantage used by the actor term.

questions.q: What does PPO's clipped objective prevent?
options: Policy updates that move the probability ratio far outside [1 - ε, 1 + ε] in the direction that would increase the objective
questions.why: The objective is $\min(r A, \text{clip}(r, 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A)$, a pessimistic bound that removes the incentive to over-move.

questions.q: Why can PPO reuse each batch of data for several epochs while vanilla policy gradient can't?
options: The clipped ratio keeps the updated policy near the one that collected the data, so the samples stay approximately valid
Vanilla PG uses too large a batch
questions.why: Plain PG on stale data takes steps that the old samples no longer justify. The clip, often with a KL check, limits this.

questions.q: Why are advantages often normalised within a batch?
options: It keeps the gradient scale stable across batches and tasks
It is required for the value loss
It changes the sign of the gradient
questions.why: Normalising to zero mean and unit variance acts as an adaptive baseline and step size. It slightly changes the objective but helps in practice.

questions.q: A Bradley-Terry reward model is trained on pairs. What is its loss for a chosen response $y_w$ and rejected $y_l$?
questions.why: Only the difference matters, so rewards are defined up to a constant per prompt. That is why they are often normalised before RL.

questions.q: Why is a KL penalty against the reference (SFT) model used in RLHF?
options: To make the reward model larger
To remove the need for a value function
To stop the policy exploiting reward model errors and drifting into text the reward model never saw
questions.why: The reward is $r - \beta \log(\pi/\pi_{ref})$ per sample. Without it the policy finds outputs that score high but read badly.

questions.q: What does DPO optimise instead of running RL?
options: A classification loss on preference pairs using the log-ratio of policy to reference probabilities as an implicit reward
A PPO objective with a fixed reward
The SFT loss on chosen responses only
questions.why: The loss is $-\log\sigma(\beta[\log\frac{\pi(y_w)}{\pi_{ref}(y_w)} - \log\frac{\pi(y_l)}{\pi_{ref}(y_l)}])$, derived from the closed-form optimum of the KL-regularised objective.

questions.q: In DPO, what does increasing β do?
options: Lets the policy move further from the reference
Keeps the policy closer to the reference model
questions.why: β is the weight of the KL term in the objective DPO is derived from, so a larger β penalises drift from the reference more strongly.

questions.q: How does GRPO estimate advantages without a value network?
options: It trains a critic on the side
It uses the reward directly with no baseline
It samples a group of responses per prompt and standardises each reward by the group's mean and standard deviation
It uses the reference model's log-probability
questions.why: The group mean acts as the baseline. This saves the memory and compute of a separate critic as large as the policy.

questions.q: What baseline does RLOO use for sample i out of k?
options: The mean reward of all k samples including i
The mean reward of the other k - 1 samples for the same prompt
The maximum reward in the group
questions.why: Leaving sample i out keeps the baseline independent of its own action, so the gradient estimate stays unbiased.

questions.q: What is "reward hacking" in RLHF?
options: The policy finds outputs that score highly under the learned reward model but aren't actually better
The reward model is trained on too much data
questions.why: Common symptoms are length growth, flattery and repeated phrases the reward model happens to like.

questions.q: In PPO for RLHF, at what granularity is the KL penalty usually applied?
options: Per token, while the reward model's score is added at the final token
questions.why: Each generated token is an action. The per-token KL term gives dense feedback; the sequence-level reward arrives at the end.
